prompt_free_text:
This paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a modification of Transformer self-attention intended to encode recursive syntactic state through an explicit stack-like mechanism. The core idea is to maintain a “stack tape” of token depths under an incremental shift-reduce style parse, supervise attachment decisions from silver constituency parses, and use the resulting depth values to additively bias attention logits. Empirically, the paper reports gains on Dyck generalization, syntactic evaluation benchmarks such as BLIMP and SG, improved sample efficiency on a parsed Wikipedia corpus, and modest downstream gains when finetuning GPT-2 with Pushdown Layers. Overall, I found the paper interesting, technically nontrivial, and potentially impactful. The main strengths are the elegance of the architectural idea, the attempt to preserve parallel training despite introducing structured state, and the breadth of empirical evaluation. At the same time, several aspects of the method and evaluation need sharper clarification, and some of the strongest claims should be tempered because the approach relies heavily on supervised or silver syntax and incurs substantial memory/inference overhead.

The paper’s central contribution is conceptually appealing. Rather than linearizing parse actions into extra tokens, as in prior syntactic language models, the model keeps the original token sequence and injects structural information directly into attention through depth-conditioned key offsets. This is a nice design point between unconstrained Transformers and more rigid transition-based structured LMs. I also appreciate that the authors frame the method as a soft inductive bias rather than a hard masking scheme. The stack tape abstraction is intuitive, and the synchronous prediction of words and attachment decisions is a meaningful departure from prior action-sequence models. If the method works as advertised, it offers a practically useful way to incorporate recursive bias without tripling sequence length.

The empirical results are promising. The Dyck experiments are a good sanity check and support the claim that the architecture helps with recursive generalization beyond what a multitask baseline gets from attachment supervision alone. On sentence-level language modeling, the gains on BLIMP and SG over an unconstrained Transformer are substantial, and the comparison to PLM/TG is relevant. The WikiTrees experiments are also valuable because they move beyond small curated corpora and suggest improved sample efficiency at larger scale. The GPT-2 finetuning experiment, while modest, helps argue that the layer can be inserted into pretrained models and may transfer beyond pure syntactic evaluation.

That said, I have several concerns about the framing and evidence. The biggest is that the method’s benefits may derive at least as much from explicit supervised syntax as from the particular pushdown parameterization. The model is trained with gold/silver attachment supervision and uses precomputed stack tapes during training. This makes it difficult to disentangle whether the gains come from the architectural bias itself, from access to parse annotations, or from the auxiliary structured objective. The Dyck baseline with attachment loss helps somewhat, but for the natural language experiments the paper does not include the most important controls: for example, a standard Transformer trained with the same parse supervision but without depth-modulated attention; a model with random or corrupted stack tapes; or a simpler syntax-conditioned attention bias using parse depth or constituent boundaries without the pushdown update mechanism. Without such ablations, the paper’s claim that the explicit stack memory mechanism is the key driver remains suggestive rather than fully established.

A related issue is fairness and comparability of baselines. Table 2 compares perplexities across models with different tokenization and notes that some numbers are not directly comparable. This weakens the claim that Pushdown-LM maintains similar or slightly better perplexity than alternatives. More broadly, the structured baselines come from prior work, and it is not fully clear whether they are matched in parameter count, training budget, data preprocessing, and decoding setup. Since the paper’s main empirical message is comparative, stronger effort toward apples-to-apples baselines would improve confidence. In particular, because Pushdown Layers add parameters and use supervised parses, a stronger baseline would be a Transformer with comparable parameter increase and the same auxiliary attachment head but standard attention.

The inference story also deserves more scrutiny. Training is parallel because stack tapes are precomputed from annotated parses, but inference requires approximate marginalization over parses with beam search. This is a meaningful cost, especially for BLIMP and SG where probabilities are central. The paper argues that decoding is simpler than word-synchronous decoding in transition-based models, but beam search over latent parses is still expensive and introduces approximation error. It would help to know how sensitive results are to beam size, whether beam 300 is necessary, and how much runtime overhead this creates relative to a standard LM. Since one of the selling points is practical drop-in replacement, the paper should more transparently quantify training speed, inference speed, and memory overhead in realistic settings. The implementation section acknowledges a large memory increase from storing 3D key tensors, but the practical implications are underexplained. “Same FLOPs” is not very informative if memory bandwidth and cache behavior dominate actual throughput.

There are also some modeling choices that are under-motivated or insufficiently analyzed. The attachment decision is made by selecting the rightmost token of a constituent. This is clever operationally, but it is not obvious how robust or expressive this representation is, especially for ambiguous or non-binary structures. The paper says the parse is built as a unique sequence of stack-tape updates, but the exact mapping from constituency trees to attachment sequences deserves a clearer formal treatment, including how unary chains, n-ary branching, punctuation, and sentence boundaries are handled. Since the model is trained on silver parses in some settings, it would also be useful to know how noisy attachment supervision affects learning. The parsing analysis in Section 5 is interesting, but because the model is trained on parser-produced annotations and evaluated partly against binarized versions of those structures, the parsing result is not strong evidence of independent syntactic induction.

Another concern is the scope of the claims. The paper sometimes suggests that Pushdown Layers address recursion more generally, potentially relevant to reasoning, programming, or planning. But the actual method is tightly tied to constituency parses and English syntax, as the limitations section partly acknowledges. The current evidence supports a narrower claim: supervised constituency-informed attention biases improve syntactic generalization in English language modeling. I would encourage the authors to moderate broader statements about recursion unless they provide experiments outside constituency parsing or natural language. The Dyck experiment is helpful, but it still uses explicit structural supervision.

The downstream finetuning results are encouraging but not yet compelling. The gains on GLUE are small and limited to 3 of 4 tasks, with one task slightly worse. Since the procedure requires first finetuning on parsed WikiText and then precomputing stack tapes for each downstream dataset, it is not obvious that the benefit justifies the added complexity. It would help to report variance, significance, and perhaps a stronger set of tasks where syntax is known to matter. As presented, this section is more of a proof of compatibility than a strong demonstration of practical utility.

I also found some technical details insufficiently specified for full reproducibility from the main text. For example, how are depth embeddings parameterized and clipped for large depths? Are they shared across heads or layers? How are sentence boundaries handled in long-context WikiTrees training? How exactly are multi-sentence contexts parsed and merged? What is the loss weighting between LM and attachment supervision? During GPT-2 adaptation, are all parameters finetuned jointly after replacing layers, or are some frozen? These may be in the appendix, but several are important enough to summarize in the main paper.

Despite these concerns, I think the paper has real merit. The architectural idea is novel relative to prior syntax-aware Transformers, and the results on syntactic benchmarks are strong enough to suggest that the method is doing something meaningful. I especially like that the approach preserves the original token sequence rather than expanding it with structural actions, and that the structural bias enters attention in a soft, learnable way. The paper is also generally well written and motivated, with intuitive figures.

To strengthen the work, I would most strongly recommend additional ablations and controls. First, compare against a standard Transformer with identical attachment supervision and parameter count but no stack-tape-conditioned attention. Second, test corrupted, shuffled, or depth-only stack tapes to isolate whether the pushdown update dynamics matter beyond generic syntax features. Third, report sensitivity to beam size and practical runtime/memory costs at training and inference. Fourth, analyze robustness to parser noise by varying the quality of silver parses or mixing gold and silver supervision. Fifth, if possible, include a partially unsupervised or latent-structure variant, even if preliminary, to show the architecture is not fundamentally dependent on external parses.

In summary, I view this as a strong and creative paper with a meaningful contribution, but one whose causal claims are not yet fully nailed down by the current experiments. The evidence convincingly shows that syntax-supervised Pushdown Layers improve syntactic generalization over a plain Transformer. It is less clear that the explicit pushdown mechanism itself, rather than supervised structural side information more broadly, is the decisive factor. If the authors can address the ablation and efficiency questions, this would be a very solid contribution.

My overall recommendation is positive but not without reservations. I would lean toward acceptance if the conference values architectural innovation and syntax-aware language modeling, though I think the paper would benefit substantially from stronger controls and a more careful presentation of scope and practical tradeoffs.

prompt_structured_json.summary: The paper proposes Pushdown Layers, a replacement for standard self-attention that augments Transformer language models with an explicit stack-like memory represented as a per-prefix stack tape of token depths in an incremental constituency parse. The model jointly predicts next tokens and attachment decisions, using supervised silver/gold parses to update the stack tape and to bias attention through depth embeddings added to keys. Empirically, the method improves generalization on Dyck languages, syntactic evaluation benchmarks (BLIMP and SG test suites), and sample efficiency on a large automatically parsed Wikipedia corpus, while maintaining similar perplexity to a baseline Transformer. The paper also reports modest gains when finetuning GPT-2 with Pushdown Layers on several GLUE tasks and presents parsing analyses showing competitive unlabeled F1.
strengths: The paper addresses an important limitation of standard self-attention for recursive structure and proposes a clear, intuitively motivated architectural bias based on stack-like state tracking.

The method is novel in combining incremental shift-reduce style structural state with Transformer attention without expanding the token sequence with explicit structural actions during standard forward computation.
The stack-tape mechanism is conceptually elegant: it provides a compact structural summary that can softly modulate attention rather than imposing hard masks.
Empirical evaluation is broad, spanning synthetic formal languages, sentence-level language modeling, larger-scale Wikipedia pretraining, downstream GLUE finetuning, and parsing-oriented analysis.
Results on syntactic generalization are strong and generally convincing, especially on Dyck generalization and SG/BLIMP relative to a standard Transformer baseline.
The comparison to prior structured language models is thoughtful, highlighting the advantage of not tripling sequence length with explicit transition tokens.
The paper is well written overall, with helpful figures and a reasonably transparent description of the stack update mechanism and training/inference setup.
The reported sample-efficiency gains on WikiTrees are practically interesting and support the claim that explicit structural bias can help in lower-data regimes.
weaknesses: The approach depends on supervised constituency parses, often silver parses from an external parser, which weakens claims about intrinsic modeling improvements and limits applicability across languages/domains.

The method is not truly a drop-in replacement in practical deployment: inference requires maintaining and searching over latent parses/attachments, and evaluation of sentence probabilities relies on approximate beam marginalization.
The computational and memory overhead is substantial due to 3D key tensors, yet runtime and scalability tradeoffs are not thoroughly quantified in experiments.

Several empirical comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples, especially perplexity comparisons against prior work with different tokenization and the GLUE staged finetuning setup that introduces parser-derived supervision.
The downstream GLUE gains are small and inconsistent, with one task worsening, so the broader utility beyond syntactic benchmarks remains limited.
The paper does not sufficiently disentangle whether gains come from the architectural bias itself, the auxiliary attachment supervision, or simply access to parse annotations during training.
The representation of recursive state via token depths may be too coarse to capture richer syntactic distinctions; the paper does not analyze failure cases where depth alone is insufficient.
The claim of broader applicability to non-syntactic phenomena such as topical dependencies or coreference is speculative and unsupported by experiments.
methodological_flaws: There is a train-test mismatch: during training, attention uses precomputed ground-truth stack tapes, whereas at inference the model conditions on its own predicted attachments/parses. This exposure bias could materially affect results, but the paper does not quantify the gap or provide ablations comparing teacher-forced versus predicted stack tapes during evaluation.

The probabilistic formulation in Eq. (7) defines a joint model over words and parses, but most reported evaluations of p(x) rely on approximate beam marginalization over a restricted parse subset. Because beam size and search errors can strongly affect results, especially BLIMP/SG comparisons, empirical validity depends on decoding quality that is not systematically analyzed.

The attachment mechanism uses argmax decisions to update the stack tape during inference, making the structural state discrete and non-differentiable. While training sidesteps this with supervised tapes, this means the model does not learn under its own induced latent structure, weakening the scientific claim that the architecture itself robustly learns recursive computation.

The claim in the implementation section that Pushdown Layers require the same number of operations as standard self-attention is incomplete/misleading: although arithmetic complexity of the batched multiplication may be similar, constructing and storing per-query depth-conditioned keys changes memory traffic substantially and likely affects effective computational cost. The paper acknowledges practical slowdown but does not provide rigorous complexity/runtime benchmarks.

Comparisons to prior structured models on perplexity are explicitly not comparable due to tokenization differences, yet these numbers are still presented in the main results table, which can invite overinterpretation.

The parsing evaluation is potentially biased because the training data are annotated by an external parser and evaluation includes comparison to that parser on auto-parsed BLLIP data; high agreement there does not necessarily demonstrate true parsing quality. Even on PTB, filtering out OOV-containing sentences changes the evaluation set and complicates comparison.

The GLUE experiments use a staged pipeline where parses are first obtained from the finetuned model and then used to precompute stack tapes for classification finetuning. This introduces extra task-specific preprocessing and supervision not available to the baseline in a strictly equivalent architectural sense, making causal attribution of gains less clean.

The paper lacks key ablations: number/location of Pushdown Layers, effect of removing attachment supervision while keeping depth-biased attention, effect of noisy versus gold parses, and sensitivity to beam size. Without these, it is hard to isolate which components are necessary for the reported gains.
